title: Did the salt even out the partitions?
prompt: Prove what salting does to the busiest partition. Write `solve(api_requests)` so it returns one row: `requests`, then `busiest_before` and `busiest_after`, the most rows any one partition holds when the requests are shuffled into 4 partitions by `endpoint`, and by `endpoint` and `salt`.
rules: `busiest_before`: repartition into 4 partitions by `endpoint`. `busiest_after`: add `salt`, the remainder of `F.hash("request_id")` by 4 (0 to 3), and repartition into 4 partitions by `endpoint` and `salt`.
Each is the largest number of rows in one partition. Requests with no endpoint count like any other. With no requests at all, both are missing.
`requests` counts all requests. Keep the setting in the starter. Return the one row from the `spark.createDataFrame` line.
hints: `groupBy(F.spark_partition_id())` counts the rows per partition; `agg(F.max(...))` on that keeps the largest.
`.collect()[0][0]` turns a one-row, one-column result into a Python value, and it's `None` when there were no rows to take a maximum of.
Salt with `F.pmod(F.hash("request_id"), F.lit(4))`, then `repartition(4, "endpoint", "salt")` hashes both columns together.
explanation: Shuffling by `endpoint` sends every row of a key to one partition, so the busiest partition holds at least the hot key's rows. With `(endpoint, salt)` as the key, the hot endpoint's rows hash to up to four places, and on a skewed table the busiest partition shrinks. On tiny inputs it can go either way: which partition a group lands in is still up to the hash, so the busiest one can even grow. That's why you measure instead of assuming. These counts are a fact about where the rows go, the same on every run with adaptive execution off; they say nothing about time in this two-core environment. The maximum over no partitions is missing, so the empty case needs no special code.
